eu_ai_act_overview.title: The EU AI Act at a glance
eu_ai_act_overview.content: The EU Artificial Intelligence Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) is the world's first comprehensive, horizontal legal framework for artificial intelligence. It follows a risk-based approach: AI systems are sorted into four tiers. Unacceptable-risk systems (for example social scoring by public authorities) are banned outright. High-risk systems are subject to strict requirements such as risk management, data governance, human oversight, logging and conformity assessment. Limited-risk systems carry transparency duties, for example disclosing that content is AI-generated. Minimal-risk systems face no new obligations. A separate chapter regulates general-purpose AI (GPAI) models: large models, such as LLMs, that can serve many downstream applications. Providers of GPAI models face documentation and transparency duties, with stricter obligations for models classified as posing systemic risk. Enforcement lies with national authorities and the newly created European AI Office. Penalties can reach 35 million euros or 7 percent of global annual turnover, whichever is higher.

gpai_obligations.title: Obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models
gpai_obligations.content: Obligations for providers of general-purpose AI (GPAI) models under the EU AI Act. Article 53 sets four baseline duties for every GPAI provider: (1) draw up and keep up to date technical documentation of the model, including its training and testing process and evaluation results; (2) provide information and documentation to downstream providers who integrate the model into their own AI systems, so that they can comply with their own obligations; (3) put in place a policy to comply with EU copyright law, including the reservation of rights under the text-and-data-mining exception; (4) publish a sufficiently detailed public summary of the content used for training, using a template provided by the AI Office. Providers of GPAI models with systemic risk have additional duties under Article 55: perform model evaluations including adversarial testing, assess and mitigate systemic risks at Union level, track and report serious incidents to the AI Office, and ensure an adequate level of cybersecurity for the model and its physical infrastructure. Open-source GPAI models are exempt from duties (1) and (2) unless they pose systemic risk.

systemic_risk_threshold.title: When does a GPAI model pose systemic risk?
systemic_risk_threshold.content: Under Article 51 of the EU AI Act, a general-purpose AI model is presumed to pose systemic risk when the cumulative amount of computation used for its training exceeds 10^25 floating-point operations (FLOPs). The Commission may also designate a model as posing systemic risk based on criteria such as the number of parameters, the size of the training data set, the number of registered business users, and the model's reach in the Union market. Providers must notify the Commission within two weeks of meeting the threshold.

ai_act_timeline.title: Timeline: when the EU AI Act applies
ai_act_timeline.content: The EU AI Act entered into force on 1 August 2024. Its provisions apply in stages. Prohibitions on unacceptable-risk practices apply from 2 February 2025. Obligations for general-purpose AI models apply from 2 August 2025. Most remaining provisions apply from 2 August 2026. The obligations for high-risk systems were postponed by an amending regulation adopted in 2026 (the Digital Omnibus on AI): they apply from 2 December 2027 for stand-alone high-risk systems listed in Annex III and from 2 August 2028 for high-risk systems embedded in regulated products (Annex I).

us_executive_order.title: EU AI Act obligations for general-purpose AI models: how does the US compare?
us_executive_order.content: Providers of general-purpose AI models face binding obligations under the EU AI Act. Do providers of general-purpose AI models face comparable obligations in the United States? At federal level, no. United States Executive Order 14110 on Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy Artificial Intelligence (October 2023) required developers of the most powerful dual-use foundation models to report safety test results to the government and tasked NIST with red-teaming guidance, but it was not legislation and imposed no obligations on most providers of AI models. The order was rescinded in January 2025 and replaced by an executive order that emphasises innovation and the removal of regulatory barriers. US federal policy has thus swung between voluntary commitments, reporting duties for frontier models and deregulation, while the EU AI Act remains a binding, risk-tiered regulation. The more interesting obligations for providers of AI models in the US now come from the states. Anyone who wants to understand what providers of general-purpose AI models really have to do should read the full story: [us_federal_ai_policy] for the federal level and [us_state_ai_laws] for the state level.

us_federal_ai_policy.title: US federal AI policy since 2025: from safety reporting to deregulation
us_federal_ai_policy.content: Since January 2025, US federal policy on artificial intelligence has turned towards deregulation. Executive Order 14179, Removing Barriers to American Leadership in Artificial Intelligence, revoked the earlier safety-oriented order and told agencies to review the measures taken under it. America's AI Action Plan of July 2025 rests on three pillars: accelerating innovation, building American AI infrastructure, and leading in international diplomacy and security. None of this creates binding duties for developers of large models; model evaluations by the Center for AI Standards and Innovation at NIST are voluntary. At the end of 2025 the federal government also began to challenge state laws on AI that it regards as barriers to innovation. The next question is therefore what the states require: see [us_state_ai_laws].

us_state_ai_laws.title: US state laws on AI: Colorado, California, Texas
us_state_ai_laws.content: In the absence of a federal statute, US states have passed their own laws on artificial intelligence. Colorado's AI Act of 2024 was the first broad state law on high-risk AI systems; it places duties of reasonable care against algorithmic discrimination on developers and deployers, and its start was postponed to 2026. California's Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act of 2025 requires large developers of frontier models to publish a safety framework and to report critical safety incidents. The Texas Responsible Artificial Intelligence Governance Act, in force since January 2026, prohibits a list of intentionally harmful uses. No state law has the scope of the European regulation, and the patchwork keeps changing: for the federal reaction see [us_federal_ai_policy].

pasta_carbonara.title: Classic Roman pasta carbonara
pasta_carbonara.content: Classic Roman carbonara uses guanciale, eggs, pecorino romano and black pepper. There is no cream in a traditional carbonara. Render the guanciale slowly, whisk yolks with grated pecorino, and combine off the heat so the eggs thicken without scrambling. Reserve a cup of starchy pasta water to loosen the sauce. Spaghetti or rigatoni both work well.
